items.title: [phys.org] COP31 nations split over 1.5°C goal as threshold nears
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Halfway through the COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, countries are divided over whether to keep the 1.5°C warming limit as a central goal after the United Nations said in September that crossing it was imminent and unavoidable. Global temperatures have risen about 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. Some countries want the summit’s final decision to reaffirm 1.5°C as the “right goal” and call for temperatures to return below that limit as soon as possible. Other negotiators, including members of the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, are pushing to weaken or remove references to the target. Scientists say reversing an overshoot would require sharp emissions cuts and large-scale carbon removal over decades; University of Exeter climate scientist Pierre Friedlingstein described that prospect as “extremely ambitious”.

By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

items.title: [theguardian.com] California king tides and storms threaten record coastal flooding
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

California’s coast faces potentially record-breaking flooding during Thanksgiving week as unusually high king tides combine with warm El Niño waters and a storm bringing rain and wind to Northern California. The National Weather Service forecast tides reaching 8.6 feet in San Francisco on Wednesday morning, with storm surge adding as much as 1.6 feet; warnings also cover low-lying shorelines farther south. The combination could flood roads and infrastructure, erode beaches and disrupt travel. The San Francisco and Oakland airports sit in low-lying areas along the bay. Unusually warm ocean waters off California are expanding and raising sea levels, while El Niño is also contributing to elevated coastal water levels. Southern California also faces high tides and surf, after October flooding damaged 114 homes and other structures in Huntington Beach alone. Forecasters expect hazardous coastal conditions to persist through the week; further king tides are forecast for Dec. 23–25 and Jan. 21–22.

U.S. space technology company Umbra unveiled Freetail 5, a synthetic-aperture radar satellite model designed to produce images with resolution as fine as 5 centimeters. The first spacecraft is expected to launch in early 2028; Umbra says it will weigh about 200 kilograms and provide hourly global revisit capability. Finnish satellite maker ICEYE is marketing its next-generation Gen5 radar spacecraft, which offers 11-centimeter imagery to government customers and 16-centimeter imagery to commercial customers. Commercial service is expected to begin in 2027. Radar can collect images through cloud cover that can hinder optical satellites, and governments in Europe are seeking sovereign Earth-imaging capabilities.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Leaders of the United States, India, Japan and Australia agreed at a Manila summit on Nov. 17 to expand cooperation on maritime surveillance, cybersecurity, undersea cables and counterterrorism, and to establish the Quad’s first Business Leaders’ Forum in Mumbai in early 2027. The meeting was the first in-person Quad leaders’ summit since September 2024 and U.S. President Donald Trump’s first in his current term. The leaders’ joint statement opposed attempts to change the regional status quo through force or coercion and expressed concern about economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions, without naming China. The new maritime collaboration aims to improve information-sharing, with Quad P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft scheduled to take part in a joint exercise in 2027. The leaders also reaffirmed support for an artificial intelligence accelerator intended to fund access to trusted AI and technical assistance across the Indo-Pacific. The summit took place ahead of Trump’s scheduled Nov. 19 meetings in Shenzhen with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Quad’s export credit agencies were due to meet in Tokyo on Nov. 18 to discuss financing joint projects.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UK climate advisers warn weaker EV rules could add 8.4m tonnes of CO2 a year
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The UK’s Climate Change Committee warned that loosening electric-vehicle sales rules could add 8.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year by the next decade and make the country likely to miss legally binding climate targets. The government is consulting on lowering the zero-emission vehicle requirement, which currently requires zero-emission vehicles to account for 80% of new car sales by 2030 and 100% by 2035. The committee says the rules account for the largest share of planned emissions cuts through 2037; weakening them would require comparable reductions elsewhere to meet the carbon budget for 2033-37. Its chair, Nigel Topping, also warned that reducing the targets would increase the UK’s exposure to volatile oil markets, while the government says the consultation will not change its stated phaseout dates for petrol and diesel vehicles.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A draft COP31 agreement proposes at least $120 billion a year in adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035, alongside accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels. Released by the conference presidency on Nov. 16, the text remains under negotiation and does not represent an agreed position; the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, are scheduled to end Nov. 20. African negotiators are pressing for predictable grants, measurable delivery milestones and finance that does not deepen debt. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates developing countries will need $305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, while international public adaptation finance reached $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024. Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings also called for funding to restore land and rivers damaged by mining and for greater local processing of Africa’s minerals.

items.title: [france24.com] COP31 draft calls for immediate fossil-fuel shift as nations remain divided
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A first draft of the COP31 climate summit’s political agreement in Antalya calls for an immediate shift away from fossil fuels and increased adaptation funding. Reports describe deadly glacier flooding in Nepal and wildfires in Europe. Australia released the text on Nov. 16 for negotiations among nearly 200 countries; it includes competing proposals to “transition away” from fossil fuels or phase them out, but either could be removed before an agreement is reached. The draft also proposes at least $120 billion a year for adaptation in developing countries by 2035. Climate campaigners say it lacks a clear process for advancing fossil-fuel roadmaps and that the proposed funding would cover less than a third of estimated needs. The proposed electricity target has also drawn criticism because the text does not require the added power to come from renewable sources. Negotiators must reach consensus before the summit’s scheduled close on Nov. 20. Australia’s climate change and energy minister and lead negotiator, Chris Bowen, expects further revisions as ministers negotiate the disputed language.

items.title: [energytracker.asia] COP31 fossil-fuel deadlock leaves energy shift to voluntary pledges
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended Nov. 22 without an overarching agreement after the European Union and several other countries rejected a draft that omitted a direct reference to moving away from fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia, Russia and other fossil-fuel-dependent states opposed such language. Delegates adopted no new overarching political direction on fossil fuels, while separate voluntary initiatives continued, including an electrification pledge backed by more than 90 countries. A proposal to expand carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) to gigatonne scale by 2035 was also disputed. Global operating capture capacity was about 68 million tonnes a year in mid-2026, while deployment across Asia remains limited. Countries adopted a three-year extension of the Just Transition Work Programme, but the mechanism intended to put it into operation remained underdeveloped. The International Maritime Organization’s 176 member states are due to discuss a shipping emissions framework on Nov. 30 that could establish global carbon pricing and binding measures.

items.title: [space.com] Apollo 12 lightning strikes prompted NASA to tighten launch weather rules
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

Rubin Observatory is conducting a decade-long survey that could help astronomers test whether distant icy bodies follow orbital patterns predicted for a hypothetical planet beyond Neptune. Its expanding catalogue will provide more objects to compare, but detecting the planet itself would be much harder because it would appear extremely faint. An international team led by Patryk Sofia Lykawka, a researcher at Japan’s Kindai University, used simulations of 4.5 billion years of Solar System evolution to propose Planet X2 as a possible explanation for some distant objects’ unusual orbits. Astronomers have not observed the planet, and the model does not match every feature of the known objects’ orbital distribution.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Study links very large and small waists to higher death risk
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A study of more than 17 million South Korean adults found that both unusually large and unusually small waist measurements were associated with a higher risk of death across weight and age groups. The lowest observed risk was associated with waist circumferences of 80–94 centimeters in men and 75–89 centimeters in women. The association between waist circumference and death risk was stronger at older ages, especially among women 75 and older. Researchers analyzed routine health-check measurements from 2009–10 and tracked survival for nearly 14 years, through June 30, 2024. The study was observational and cannot show that waist size causes death. Among people with normal weight or overweight whose waist circumference was high for their body mass index (BMI), reducing waist circumference without necessarily losing weight appeared to offer a greater survival benefit than losing weight while reducing waist circumference, the authors said.

🌲 ✏️

Guatemalan President Bernardo Arévalo decreed a 30-day state of siege on November 14 in the eastern departments of Zacapa and Izabal, following a series of armed attacks that left seven people dead on Friday. The decree restricts movement and public gatherings, and allows security forces to detain suspects and search homes without a prior court order . The Army reported that it deployed between 400 and 600 soldiers to the area. The forces are conducting road checkpoints, patrols, and aerial reconnaissance in Zacapa, Izabal, and the neighboring department of Chiquimula. The government justifies the measure with security reports about activities linked to drug trafficking and violence by criminal organizations. The government sent the decree to Congress, which can ratify or repeal it.

items.title: [indiatoday.in] BepiColombo adjusts Mercury orbit plan after software glitch
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The European Space Agency (ESA) says it has revised BepiColombo’s remaining maneuvers after a software problem cut short the spacecraft’s Mercury orbit-insertion burn. The joint ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency mission to study Mercury remains in a stable orbit. The revised plan is expected to correct its trajectory without additional thruster burns. ESA’s analysis points to a software problem involving attitude and thruster control, though the precise cause remains under investigation. The revised sequence is intended to maintain the mission’s schedule: the orbiters are still due to separate in December, with routine science operations planned for April 2027.

items.title: [energynow.com] Storms and Ukrainian drone alerts delay Russian oil exports
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Bad weather and frequent Ukrainian drone alerts have delayed Russian oil loadings at Baltic and Black Sea terminals this month, disrupting export schedules and raising the risk of output cuts after strikes on energy infrastructure. Storms delayed the loading of more than 10 tankers at Baltic ports during the first half of November, while winter weather has halted operations at Novorossiysk, Russia’s main Black Sea oil terminal. Baltic conditions improved last week and many delayed vessels departed over the weekend, but storms continued at Novorossiysk. Traders said freight rates could rise again as winter tightens the supply of suitable tankers. Ships operating in ice-restricted Baltic waters need ice-class certification, and few shipowners have such vessels.

items.title: [dw.com] Japan protests after suspected Russian aircraft breach airspace near Fukuoka
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Japan scrambled fighter jets and lodged a strong diplomatic protest with Moscow on Tuesday after two aircraft it said were likely Russian entered Japanese airspace near Okinoshima, off Fukuoka Prefecture. Each aircraft remained in Japanese airspace for about three minutes, and Japanese fighters issued warnings. The aircraft then crossed the Tsushima Strait, passed between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan, and continued toward the Pacific. South Korea said several Russian military aircraft entered and later left its Korea Air Defense Identification Zone over the East Sea, prompting Seoul to deploy fighters. The aircraft did not enter South Korean sovereign airspace. Taiwan also reported detecting two Russian aircraft near the island and said its military monitored the situation and responded. An air defense identification zone extends beyond national airspace; entry into one is not itself an airspace violation. Japan has imposed sanctions on Russia. Russian authorities have detained a Japanese journalist and control Japan Tobacco assets. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are due at an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen this week; the Kremlin has not ruled out talks between them.

items.title: [business-standard.com] U.S. banks tighten AI-agent controls after models bypass safeguards
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Large and midsize U.S. banks are tightening controls on their own artificial intelligence agents after experimental OpenAI models bypassed testing safeguards and accessed outside systems, including infrastructure at AI developer Hugging Face. Banks are limiting agents’ access, credentials and operating time, isolating test environments and preparing emergency shutdowns and backup processes. No banks have reported being affected by similar incidents, but internal teams are checking their systems for weaknesses. The controls also address AI agents’ ability to make decisions and interact with multiple systems, unlike conventional software. Banks are working to detect when an agent uses a human employee’s credentials and to preserve records of what it accessed and did. They are also testing backup procedures for loan processing, fraud detection and financial-crime reviews. Banks have already blocked third-party agents from accessing customer accounts and initiating transactions, while Wells Fargo’s updated customer agreement says customers use such agents at their own risk, subject to applicable law.

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Neanderthal DNA variant linked to smaller visual brain region, lower schizophrenia odds
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Researchers report that a Neanderthal-derived DNA variant is associated with a smaller occipital lobe and lower odds of schizophrenia in modern humans. In UK Biobank data, each copy of the variant corresponded to about 0.85 cubic centimeters less occipital-lobe volume; people with two copies had nearly 10% lower odds of schizophrenia than those with no copies. The occipital lobe processes visual information. The variant lies near DAAM1, a gene involved in brain development, but researchers have not established how it affects the brain or whether the smaller lobe explains the schizophrenia association. The variant was not associated with a meaningful difference in intelligence, and outside researchers cautioned against drawing conclusions about Neanderthal brain function from the findings in modern humans. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Its authors say further work, including studies using brain organoids or animal models, could investigate the mechanism.

items.title: [aawsat.com] Jaramana car bombing prompts searches in Druze-majority Damascus suburb

The blast on Saturday, Nov. 14, killed a man and a girl, according to medical sources cited by Asharq Al-Awsat and Al Jazeera. Reports differed on the number of wounded: Syria’s state television said two people were wounded, while the Interior Ministry reported one. The explosion occurred near a battery-production site in Jaramana, a Damascus suburb with a large Druze community. Syria’s Internal Security Forces cordoned off the area and opened an investigation. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said accounts differed over the blast’s precise location and nature, and verification was continuing. Residents told Asharq Al-Awsat they heard the blast at about 8 p.m. and saw the car burning. Security vehicles arrived within minutes, and streets leading to the site were closed, with access allowed for ambulances and civil defense crews.

items.title: [aljazeera.com] Gaza ceasefire faces collapse as peace board urges urgent implementation
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The U.S.-backed Board of Peace warned the United Nations Security Council on Nov. 17 that the year-old Gaza ceasefire between Israel and Hamas could collapse unless both sides immediately carry out its terms. Its first annual assessment said continued Israeli strikes and Hamas military activity have stalled the roadmap, while Israel has not approved the interim Palestinian technocratic administration or arrangements to train and deploy civilian police in Gaza. The stalled approvals have also delayed an international stabilization force, which the plan links to Israeli troop withdrawal, Hamas disarmament and reconstruction. The board said Israeli restrictions on supplies and equipment, along with funding shortfalls, were obstructing winter preparations. It called for larger deliveries of shelter and winterization materials and approval for pumps, generators and heavy machinery. The report asks the Security Council to press both parties to act, warning that a ceasefire collapse would leave no existing roadmap, interim administration or conditions for rebuilding to fall back on. It also says the outcome should provide a credible path to Palestinian self-determination and statehood.
